rows.Description: Big hub around the world's busiest train station: skyscrapers, neon, shopping, and nightlife like Golden Gai and Omoide Yokocho.
Huge electronics chain; the Shinjuku West flagship spans several buildings of cameras, gadgets, watches, and more.
rows.Notes: Tax refund with passport

rows.Description: Major electronics and camera chain, right by Shinjuku Station's west exit. They also sell lots of watches!
rows.Notes: Tax refund with passport

rows.Description: Cluster of new and used camera shops by Shinjuku Station's west exit, incl. Map Camera and vintage dealers.
Small family-run Japanese green tea shop, run by a certified tea appraiser, known for its rich matcha soft serve; also sells loose-leaf tea and matcha powder.
rows.Notes: In the Odakyu Ace underground mall at Shinjuku Station's west exit, near Camera Town

rows.Description: Tiny 17-seat apothecary-style bar where Hiroyasu Kayama makes cocktails from herbs he grows on his own farm; No. 18 on The World's 50 Best Bars 2025.
rows.Notes: ~15 seats; reserve ahead (TableCheck), walk-ins hard; herbs grown on the bartender’s own farm; No. 18 World’s 50 Best Bars 2025

rows.Description: Alley of tiny yakitori stalls and izakayas by Shinjuku Station's west exit, nicknamed "Memory Lane."
rows.Notes: Good for a cheap dinner before bars; many stalls are cash-only and seat only a few people

rows.Description: A few narrow alleys packed with around 200 tiny bars, each seating only a handful of people, many with their own quirky theme.
rows.Notes: Evenings only; many bars charge a cover, and some are regulars-only or ban photos, so check the signs on the door

rows.Description: Tokyo's neon nightlife district of bars, restaurants, and clubs, home to the life-size Godzilla head on Hotel Gracery.
rows.Notes: Best for a walk through at night; ignore touts trying to pull you into bars

rows.Description: Chaotic discount chain stacked floor to ceiling with snacks, souvenirs, cosmetics, and oddities.
rows.Notes: Kabukicho and Dotonbori branches are open 24/7 (Dotonbori has a Ferris wheel on the building and a duty-free counter); other branches vary, many closing around 3–5 AM. Also in Shibuya and Akihabara; tax refund with passport

rows.Description: Retro multi-floor shopping arcade packed with anime and manga collectibles (incl. many Mandarake shops) and one of Tokyo's biggest clusters of used and vintage watch dealers.
rows.Notes: Watch dealers are mostly on the 3rd floor, e.g. Jackroad (English-speaking staff, prices displayed) and Kamekichi; about 5 min by train from Shinjuku; many shops offer tax refund with passport. Watch hunt: Nakano (vintage/used) and Yodobashi/Bic (new) are substitutes — if the watch turns up at one, the others aren't needed

rows.Description: Youth fashion and nightlife district around Shibuya Station and its famous scramble crossing.
The famous scramble crosswalk where huge crowds cross from every direction at once.
rows.Notes: Best viewed from above, e.g. Shibuya Sky

rows.Description: Dogenzaka slope packed with themed love hotels, plus clubs and live music venues.
Open-air rooftop observation deck on Shibuya Scramble Square, looking straight down on the crossing.
rows.Notes: Sunset slots sell out; must book in advance

rows.Description: Japanese eyewear chain known for affordable prescription glasses; the Shibuya store is the flagship.
rows.Notes: From ~¥6,600, often ready in ~30 min; tax refund with passport

rows.Description: Multi-floor lifestyle store (formerly Tokyu Hands) for well-made everyday things: household goods, tools, travel gear, kitchenware, stationery, bath and beauty.
rows.Notes: Good for nail clippers, scissors and small practical souvenirs; a short walk from Shibuya Loft; tax refund with passport

rows.Description: Hands' trendier sibling: stationery, cosmetics and skincare, character goods and seasonal gift floors.
rows.Notes: A short walk from Hands Shibuya, so easy to do both; tax refund with passport

rows.Description: Harajuku's crowded pedestrian street of kawaii fashion, crêpes, youth culture, and animal cafes (samoyed dogs, micro-pigs, etc.)
Café where you hang out with fluffy Samoyed dogs (no other breeds); free treats to feed them and free drinks. Branches on Takeshita Street and elsewhere in Harajuku.
rows.Notes: Audrey wants this. ~¥3,000/hr, last entry 7 PM; reserve online (TableCheck) or walk in ~15 min before the hour

rows.Description: Large shrine dedicated to Emperor Meiji, set in a forest behind giant wooden torii gates.
rows.Notes: Free; right next to Takeshita Street

rows.Description: Official shop for Imabari towels, Japan's certified premium cotton towels, from handkerchiefs to bath sheets; near Omotesando.
rows.Notes: Closed 2nd Tuesday of the month

rows.Description: Ring studio where you can make your own rings or order a custom one from a craftsman; workshop rings go home the same day.
rows.Notes: Open 11 AM–7 PM; also in Kyoto (Ninenzaka, Sanjo-Kawaramachi) and Osaka (Umeda, Shinsaibashi)

rows.Description: The brand's largest flagship in Japan, with Japan-exclusive models; the NIPPON MADE shop for its fully made-in-Japan line is next door.
rows.Notes: Open 11 AM–8 PM; tax refund with passport

rows.Description: Flagship of Porter (Yoshida & Co.), the Japanese bag maker, on a quiet Omotesando backstreet; full range of shoulder and sling bags, backpacks, and luggage.
rows.Notes: Also PORTER TOKYO by Tokyo Station (Marunouchi) and Kura Chika by Porter counters in department stores; tax refund with passport

rows.Description: Old-Tokyo neighborhood around Senso-ji, Tokyo's oldest temple, and the souvenir stalls of Nakamise-dori.
Tokyo's oldest temple, entered through the giant-lantern Kaminarimon gate and Nakamise-dori.
rows.Notes: Beautifully lit at night

rows.Description: Tokyo's "Kitchen Town": a long street of shops selling Japanese knives, tableware, and plastic food samples.
rows.Notes: Knife shopping guide ↗. Most shops ~10 AM–5 PM, closed Sundays — do it in the morning and avoid a Sunday

rows.Description: "Electric Town": electronics, anime, manga, retro games, and maid cafés.
Theatrical cocktail bar in Azabu-Juban run by champion bartender Yuzo Komai.
rows.Notes: Open 6 PM–3 AM, closed Wed; reservation-only (TableCheck / phone / Instagram DM), walk-ins only early evening

rows.Description: Beautiful art-focused bookstore on the 6th floor of Ginza Six, with rare art and photography books on a 30 m bookshelf, an art gallery, and a café.
Uniqlo's 12-floor Ginza flagship, with a RE.UNIQLO STUDIO counter that embroiders bags and clothes with your own design. It's also 2-3x cheaper than the US.
rows.Notes: RE.UNIQLO STUDIO counters do embroidery, patches, and sashiko from ~¥700, at Ginza, UNIQLO TOKYO (Marunouchi), and Asakusa. Turnaround varies a lot — one report says up to 3 weeks at Ginza while printing is same-day, so ask on arrival and order early in the trip

rows.Description: Five-floor global flagship of GU, Uniqlo's cheaper and trendier sister brand, a couple of minutes from Uniqlo Ginza. It's also 2-3x cheaper than the US.
rows.Notes: Prices are much lower than GU abroad; tax refund with passport. Bigger full-line GU is in Kichijoji, and there is a branch in Shinjuku Flags

rows.Description: Ginza's landmark stationery store, in business since 1904: about a dozen floors of pens, notebooks, paper, cards and desk goods, each floor themed, with a café at the top.
rows.Notes: Right in the middle of Ginza, a few minutes from Uniqlo and GU Ginza

rows.Description: MUJI's world flagship: several floors of simple household goods, clothing, travel gear and food, with a MUJI hotel and restaurant in the same building.
rows.Notes: Bigger range and lower prices than MUJI in the US; in the Ginza cluster with Uniqlo, GU and Itoya; tax refund with passport

rows.Description: Flagship of the centuries-old bedding maker Nishikawa, where staff measure your neck and build a custom pillow on the spot; you can also try its mattresses and pillows.
rows.Notes: Custom fitting ~1 h, walk-ins OK (reserve if possible); a custom pillow reportedly ~¥30,000. ⚠ This COREDO Nihonbashi branch closes ~Oct 2026 for redevelopment (reopens as Tokyo Midtown Nihonbashi autumn 2027) — for the Oct 2027 trip use the Hiroo store or Daimaru Shinsaibashi (Osaka) instead

rows.Description: Immersive digital art museum where you walk barefoot through water and mirrored light rooms.
rows.Notes: Book timed tickets

rows.Description: Hayao Miyazaki's whimsical Studio Ghibli museum with exclusive short films.
rows.Notes: Reservation-only; tickets sell out fast

rows.Description: Japan Airlines' museum and guided walk through a working aircraft maintenance hangar at Haneda Airport.
rows.Notes: ~2 monorail stops from Terminal 3 (Shin-Seibijo). Earliest tour 9:30–11:40 (arrive ~9:00); closed Wed & Fri; reserve ahead, popular

rows.Description: Temple said to be the birthplace of the maneki-neko, filled with thousands of white beckoning-cat figurines left by visitors.
Inari shrine with a tunnel of ~1,000 red torii gates up a small hill — a pocket Fushimi Inari; the aviation-safety / airport-guardian shrine.
rows.Notes: 1 Keikyu stop (~5 min) + 3-min walk from Haneda; grounds open at dawn, free. Ideal on arrival before JAL Sky Museum

rows.Description: Disney park unique to Tokyo, themed around ports of the sea, incl. the Fantasy Springs area (Frozen, Tangled, Peter Pan); often called the best Disney park.
rows.Notes: Buy date-specific tickets in advance; plan a full day. About 15 min by train from Tokyo Station

rows.Description: Wide curtain of countless thin waterfalls spilling over a cliff on Mt. Fuji's southwest side, near Fujinomiya.
rows.Notes: On Mt. Fuji's southwest side, the opposite side from Kawaguchiko; plan it as the exit-morning stop toward Nagoya: Fujikyu bus Kawaguchiko → Shiraito (~1h10m, only ~3 buses/day, check the timetable) → Shin-Fuji → Kodama shinkansen to Nagoya

rows.Description: The most visited of the Fuji Five Lakes, with Mt. Fuji views across the water, lakeside cafés, and onsen hotels.
Flower park on Lake Kawaguchiko's north shore, framing Mt. Fuji across the lake.
Short cable car up Mt. Tenjo on Lake Kawaguchiko's east shore, with a viewing deck looking across the lake to Mt. Fuji.
rows.Notes: Formerly the Kachi Kachi Ropeway; 8:30–17:00 (last descent 17:20); queues 15 min to 1 h+, shortest right at opening or after ~3:30 PM; near Kawaguchiko Station

rows.Description: Five-story pagoda on a hillside above Fujiyoshida: the classic postcard view with Mt. Fuji behind it.
rows.Notes: About 400 steps up to the viewpoint; best at sunrise (~5:50 AM mid-Oct) from the Kawaguchiko ryokan: ~15 min by taxi, or Fujikyu train to Shimoyoshida + ~10 min walk for a later visit; the park is open 24 h

rows.Description: Studio Ghibli park recreating film settings (Howl's, Totoro, etc.)
rows.Notes: Must book in advance; tickets sell out instantly

rows.Description: Beautiful bookstore in Aeon Mall Noritake Garden, famous for a two-story lit bookshelf reflected in a mirrored ceiling so it looks endless; Starbucks inside.
rows.Notes: Most books are in Japanese; photos on the staircase are officially discouraged

rows.Description: Kyoto's geisha district of wooden teahouses and lantern-lit lanes like Hanamikoji.
rows.Notes: Best in the evening; respect no-photo and private-lane signs

rows.Description: Thousands of vermilion torii gates winding up Mt. Inari.
rows.Notes: Go early (~6 AM) to avoid crowds; open 24 hours; the full loop to the summit takes 2–3 hrs

rows.Description: The Golden Pavilion: a Zen temple covered in gold leaf, reflected in the pond in front of it.
Zen temple with Japan's most famous rock garden; a short trip from Kinkaku-ji.
Walking path through towering bamboo in western Kyoto.
rows.Notes: Gets very crowded; go early

rows.Description: Miffy-themed bakery and gift shop near the bamboo grove, selling Miffy-shaped anpan and pastries plus exclusive Kyoto pottery and kitchen goods.
rows.Notes: Short walk from Arashiyama Station; open daily, but the bakery often sells out by around 11 AM, so go early. Takeaway or standing counter only

rows.Description: Hillside temple with a huge wooden stage overlooking Kyoto, reached via the old Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka lanes.
Shogun's castle with ornate painted rooms and "nightingale floors" that squeak to warn of intruders.
Narrow covered food market known as "Kyoto's Kitchen": pickles, skewers, sweets, and kitchen knives.
Narrow lantern-lit alley along the Kamo River, lined with restaurants, bars, and teahouses.
rows.Notes: Good area for kaiseki

rows.Description: Temple hall about 120 m long holding 1,001 golden statues of Kannon.
Quiet stone path along a canal, linking temples between Ginkaku-ji and Nanzen-ji.
rows.Notes: Tons of people go here for Cherry Blossom season

rows.Description: Mossy hillside temple with 1,200 stone figures, each with its own funny expression, carved by amateur visitors.
rows.Notes: Pair with the Bamboo Grove

rows.Description: Short street of historic matcha shops and cafés — Nakamura Tokichi, Itoh Kyuemon and Tsuen (founded 1160) are all within a few minutes of each other, selling matcha, soft serve and tea sweets.
rows.Notes: 10 min walk from JR Uji station, on the JR Nara line between Kyoto (20 min) and Nara (30–40 min). Cafés queue up — takeout soft serve keeps it to an hour. Byodo-in temple is at the end of the street if you want more time

rows.Description: 3.6 km pine-covered sandbar across a bay, one of Japan's Three Scenic Views; tradition is to view it upside down between your legs.
rows.Notes: About 2 hrs from Kyoto.. probably too far for our short stay in Kyoto

rows.Description: Large park where over a thousand free-roaming deer bow for deer crackers.
Temple with a giant bronze Buddha inside one of the world's largest wooden buildings in Nara Park.
Shrine famous for its thousands of stone and bronze lanterns, in the forest at the east end of Nara Park.
Mochi shop famous for its lightning-fast mochi pounding shows, selling fresh mugwort (yomogi) mochi.
rows.Notes: No fixed show times; pounding usually stops by 3 PM

rows.Description: Canal-side strip of neon signs and street food (takoyaki, okonomiyaki), home of the Glico running man sign.
Iconic castle (a modern rebuild) with a museum inside, surrounded by moats and a big park.
Universal Studios Japan, incl. Super Nintendo World and Harry Potter.
rows.Notes: Must book in advance; the express pass is WORTH IT

rows.Description: Osaka's answer to Akihabara in Nipponbashi: anime, figures, retro games, and electronics.
"Osaka's Kitchen": covered market with fresh seafood, wagyu skewers, and street snacks.
rows.Notes: Touristy and pricey but fun

rows.Description: Long covered shopping arcade running north from Dotonbori.
Two skyscrapers joined at the top by the Floating Garden Observatory, an open-air rooftop ring with 360° views over Osaka.
rows.Notes: Open-air rooftop; best at sunset or night

rows.Description: Retro observation tower and symbol of the old-school Shinsekai neighborhood, known for kushikatsu; home of the lucky Billiken statue and a tube slide down the side.
rows.Notes: The tube slide (Tower Slider) costs extra

rows.Description: Glass-walled observation deck on the top floors of Abeno Harukas, one of Japan's tallest buildings, about 300 m up with views across Osaka.
rows.Notes: Better views than Umeda Sky; walking distance from Tsutenkaku Tower

rows.Description: Shrine whose stage is a giant lion head with an open mouth, said to swallow bad luck.
Stone-paved lantern alley by Dotonbori, home to a moss-covered Fudo statue that visitors splash with water for luck.

Retro amusement park on top of Mt. Ikoma (642 m) with views over Osaka and the Nara Basin; its Flying Tower plane ride (1929) is Japan's oldest ride still running. Reached by dog- and cat-shaped cable cars.
rows.Notes: Free entry, rides paid; open about 10 AM–5 PM, closed Thursdays, and night hours are summer only, so an October visit is daytime (check the calendar). Cable car leaves from Toriimae Station, next to Kintetsu Ikoma Station; about 30 min from Osaka

rows.Description: Mountain temple of "winning luck," covered in thousands of daruma dolls left by visitors; a 6-stamp rally around the grounds builds up a full daruma picture on a postcard.
rows.Notes: About ¥500 entry, stamp card included; the stamp rally takes 30–60 min

rows.Description: Museum at the birthplace of instant ramen, where you design your own cup and choose the soup and toppings at the My Cup Noodles Factory.
rows.Notes: Free entry; My Cup Noodles is about ¥400–500 per cup, with numbered tickets on the day; last entry 3:30 PM. Near Katsuoji

rows.Description: Former factory area turned trendy: cafés in converted warehouses, pop-up stores, and indie brands.
Upscale area with designer boutiques, galleries, and good restaurants; next to Itaewon.
Seoul's most international district: global food, bars, and nightlife.
Open library in the middle of COEX Mall, with 13 m bookshelves rising around a central seating plaza.
rows.Notes: Free

rows.Description: Bigger sibling of the COEX library inside Starfield Suwon mall (opened 2024), with 22 m bookshelves spanning four floors under a glass ceiling.
rows.Notes: Free

rows.Description: UNESCO-listed 18th-century fortress wall circling old Suwon, with grand gates, watchtowers, and a walkable path along the top of the wall.
rows.Notes: About 1 hr from Seoul by subway

rows.Description: Hillside village settled by Korean War refugees, now known for colorful painted houses, murals, and hanbok rentals.
Buddhist temple built right on the seaside cliffs.
rows.Notes: Beautiful at sunrise

rows.Description: Glass-floored U-shaped walkway over a cliff, looking out to the Oryukdo islets.
Coastal rail park; the Sky Capsules are small colorful pods that run on an elevated track along the sea.
Mountain temple on Geumjeongsan with large Buddhist figures carved into the rock face.
rows.Notes: Steep walk up

rows.Description: Beach lined with cafés and restaurants, known for its coffee street and evening views.
Easy seaside walking trail around a small wooded island, with views of Busan's skyline.
Crescent-shaped observation deck opened in 2024, reaching 134 m out over the sea off Haeundae.
rows.Notes: Free

rows.Description: Central covered market for street food, souvenirs, and clothes.
rows.Notes: Expect to bargain

rows.Description: Huge underground tunnel network used in the Vietnam War.
rows.Notes: About 1.5–2 hrs from the city

rows.Description: Backpacker nightlife strip in District 1: packed bars, loud music, and street food.
French-colonial post office from the late 1800s, next to the Notre-Dame Cathedral.
Mountaintop resort reached by a long cable car, with a French-village replica and gardens.
rows.Notes: About 1 hr from the city

rows.Description: Walkway held up by two giant stone hands, located inside Ba Na Hills.
rows.Notes: Included in the Ba Na Hills ticket

rows.Description: Son Tra Peninsula: forested hills with ocean viewpoints and rare red-shanked douc langurs.
rows.Notes: MONKEYS!!!

rows.Description: Limestone hills with caves, pagodas, and viewpoints, on the way between Da Nang and Hoi An.
Ruins of ancient Cham Hindu temples in the jungle; a UNESCO site.
rows.Notes: About 1 hr from Hoi An

rows.Description: Tall white Buddha statue at Linh Ung Pagoda on Son Tra, overlooking the bay.
Dragon-shaped bridge over the Han River that breathes fire and water.
rows.Notes: Fire and water show on weekend nights

rows.Description: Da Nang's long, wide city beach.
UNESCO-listed old trading port: lantern-lit streets, street food, tailors, riverside cafés.
rows.Notes: Best in the evening

rows.Description: Ornate Chinese assembly hall and temple built by Fujian merchants.
Colorful Chinese temple honoring the general Guan Yu, across from the central market.
Hoi An's symbol: a small covered bridge from the early 1600s.
Dense maze of streets historically named for trades, packed with street food and shops, near Hoan Kiem Lake.
Narrow residential lane where trains pass inches from cafés.
rows.Notes: Access is sometimes restricted by police

rows.Description: Ta Hien Street: a lively corner of tiny plastic stools and cheap fresh beer (bia hoi).
About 500 steps up to a dragon statue with sweeping views over the Tam Coc rice fields.
UNESCO-listed rowboat tours through limestone karsts and river caves.
Rowboat ride along a river through rice paddies and caves between limestone cliffs.
Upscale central district with cafés, cocktail bars, and the Yongkang Street food area.
Large leafy park, often called Taipei's Central Park.
World-class collection of Chinese imperial art and artifacts, incl. the famous Jadeite Cabbage.
Tea roaster in Dadaocheng since 1890; tastings, tea for sale, and tours of the roasting workshop.
Narrow hillside lanes of snack stalls, teahouses, and red lanterns.
rows.Notes: Very crowded midday

rows.Description: Traditional teahouse in a historic building, with tea service and mountain views.
Short but steep hike near Jinguashi to a teapot-shaped rock with panoramic coastal views.

Wide curtain of countless thin waterfalls spilling over a cliff on Mt. Fuji's southwest side, near Fujinomiya.

On Mt. Fuji's southwest side, the opposite side from Kawaguchiko; plan it as the exit-morning stop toward Nagoya: Fujikyu bus Kawaguchiko → Shiraito (~1h10m, only ~3 buses/day, check the timetable) → Shin-Fuji → Kodama shinkansen to Nagoya
The most visited of the Fuji Five Lakes, with Mt. Fuji views across the water, lakeside cafés, and onsen hotels.
Flower park on Lake Kawaguchiko's north shore, framing Mt. Fuji across the lake.
Short cable car up Mt. Tenjo on Lake Kawaguchiko's east shore, with a viewing deck looking across the lake to Mt. Fuji.
Formerly the Kachi Kachi Ropeway; 8:30–17:00 (last descent 17:20); queues 15 min to 1 h+, shortest right at opening or after ~3:30 PM; near Kawaguchiko Station
Five-story pagoda on a hillside above Fujiyoshida: the classic postcard view with Mt. Fuji behind it.

About 400 steps up to the viewpoint; best at sunrise (~5:50 AM mid-Oct) from the Kawaguchiko ryokan: ~15 min by taxi, or Fujikyu train to Shimoyoshida + ~10 min walk for a later visit; the park is open 24 h
Studio Ghibli park recreating film settings (Howl's, Totoro, etc.)
Must book in advance; tickets sell out instantly
Beautiful bookstore in Aeon Mall Noritake Garden, famous for a two-story lit bookshelf reflected in a mirrored ceiling so it looks endless; Starbucks inside.
Most books are in Japanese; photos on the staircase are officially discouraged
Kyoto's geisha district of wooden teahouses and lantern-lit lanes like Hanamikoji.
Best in the evening; respect no-photo and private-lane signs
Thousands of vermilion torii gates winding up Mt. Inari.
Go early (~6 AM) to avoid crowds; open 24 hours; the full loop to the summit takes 2–3 hrs
The Golden Pavilion: a Zen temple covered in gold leaf, reflected in the pond in front of it.
Zen temple with Japan's most famous rock garden; a short trip from Kinkaku-ji.
Walking path through towering bamboo in western Kyoto.
Miffy-themed bakery and gift shop near the bamboo grove, selling Miffy-shaped anpan and pastries plus exclusive Kyoto pottery and kitchen goods.
Short walk from Arashiyama Station; open daily, but the bakery often sells out by around 11 AM, so go early. Takeaway or standing counter only
Hillside temple with a huge wooden stage overlooking Kyoto, reached via the old Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka lanes.
Shogun's castle with ornate painted rooms and "nightingale floors" that squeak to warn of intruders.
Narrow covered food market known as "Kyoto's Kitchen": pickles, skewers, sweets, and kitchen knives.
Narrow lantern-lit alley along the Kamo River, lined with restaurants, bars, and teahouses.
Temple hall about 120 m long holding 1,001 golden statues of Kannon.
Quiet stone path along a canal, linking temples between Ginkaku-ji and Nanzen-ji.
Tons of people go here for Cherry Blossom season
Mossy hillside temple with 1,200 stone figures, each with its own funny expression, carved by amateur visitors.
Short street of historic matcha shops and cafés — Nakamura Tokichi, Itoh Kyuemon and Tsuen (founded 1160) are all within a few minutes of each other, selling matcha, soft serve and tea sweets.

10 min walk from JR Uji station, on the JR Nara line between Kyoto (20 min) and Nara (30–40 min). Cafés queue up — takeout soft serve keeps it to an hour. Byodo-in temple is at the end of the street if you want more time
3.6 km pine-covered sandbar across a bay, one of Japan's Three Scenic Views; tradition is to view it upside down between your legs.
About 2 hrs from Kyoto.. probably too far for our short stay in Kyoto
Large park where over a thousand free-roaming deer bow for deer crackers.
Temple with a giant bronze Buddha inside one of the world's largest wooden buildings in Nara Park.
Shrine famous for its thousands of stone and bronze lanterns, in the forest at the east end of Nara Park.
Mochi shop famous for its lightning-fast mochi pounding shows, selling fresh mugwort (yomogi) mochi.
No fixed show times; pounding usually stops by 3 PM
Canal-side strip of neon signs and street food (takoyaki, okonomiyaki), home of the Glico running man sign.
Iconic castle (a modern rebuild) with a museum inside, surrounded by moats and a big park.
Universal Studios Japan, incl. Super Nintendo World and Harry Potter.
Must book in advance; the express pass is WORTH IT
Osaka's answer to Akihabara in Nipponbashi: anime, figures, retro games, and electronics.
"Osaka's Kitchen": covered market with fresh seafood, wagyu skewers, and street snacks.
Long covered shopping arcade running north from Dotonbori.
Two skyscrapers joined at the top by the Floating Garden Observatory, an open-air rooftop ring with 360° views over Osaka.
Open-air rooftop; best at sunset or night
Retro observation tower and symbol of the old-school Shinsekai neighborhood, known for kushikatsu; home of the lucky Billiken statue and a tube slide down the side.
The tube slide (Tower Slider) costs extra
Glass-walled observation deck on the top floors of Abeno Harukas, one of Japan's tallest buildings, about 300 m up with views across Osaka.
Better views than Umeda Sky; walking distance from Tsutenkaku Tower
Shrine whose stage is a giant lion head with an open mouth, said to swallow bad luck.
Stone-paved lantern alley by Dotonbori, home to a moss-covered Fudo statue that visitors splash with water for luck.

Retro amusement park on top of Mt. Ikoma (642 m) with views over Osaka and the Nara Basin; its Flying Tower plane ride (1929) is Japan's oldest ride still running. Reached by dog- and cat-shaped cable cars.

Free entry, rides paid; open about 10 AM–5 PM, closed Thursdays, and night hours are summer only, so an October visit is daytime (check the calendar). Cable car leaves from Toriimae Station, next to Kintetsu Ikoma Station; about 30 min from Osaka
Mountain temple of "winning luck," covered in thousands of daruma dolls left by visitors; a 6-stamp rally around the grounds builds up a full daruma picture on a postcard.
About ¥500 entry, stamp card included; the stamp rally takes 30–60 min
Museum at the birthplace of instant ramen, where you design your own cup and choose the soup and toppings at the My Cup Noodles Factory.
Free entry; My Cup Noodles is about ¥400–500 per cup, with numbered tickets on the day; last entry 3:30 PM. Near Katsuoji
Former factory area turned trendy: cafés in converted warehouses, pop-up stores, and indie brands.
Upscale area with designer boutiques, galleries, and good restaurants; next to Itaewon.
Seoul's most international district: global food, bars, and nightlife.
Open library in the middle of COEX Mall, with 13 m bookshelves rising around a central seating plaza.
Bigger sibling of the COEX library inside Starfield Suwon mall (opened 2024), with 22 m bookshelves spanning four floors under a glass ceiling.
UNESCO-listed 18th-century fortress wall circling old Suwon, with grand gates, watchtowers, and a walkable path along the top of the wall.
About 1 hr from Seoul by subway
Hillside village settled by Korean War refugees, now known for colorful painted houses, murals, and hanbok rentals.
Buddhist temple built right on the seaside cliffs.
Glass-floored U-shaped walkway over a cliff, looking out to the Oryukdo islets.
Coastal rail park; the Sky Capsules are small colorful pods that run on an elevated track along the sea.
Mountain temple on Geumjeongsan with large Buddhist figures carved into the rock face.
Beach lined with cafés and restaurants, known for its coffee street and evening views.
Easy seaside walking trail around a small wooded island, with views of Busan's skyline.
Crescent-shaped observation deck opened in 2024, reaching 134 m out over the sea off Haeundae.
Central covered market for street food, souvenirs, and clothes.
Huge underground tunnel network used in the Vietnam War.
Backpacker nightlife strip in District 1: packed bars, loud music, and street food.
French-colonial post office from the late 1800s, next to the Notre-Dame Cathedral.
Mountaintop resort reached by a long cable car, with a French-village replica and gardens.
Walkway held up by two giant stone hands, located inside Ba Na Hills.
Included in the Ba Na Hills ticket
Son Tra Peninsula: forested hills with ocean viewpoints and rare red-shanked douc langurs.
Limestone hills with caves, pagodas, and viewpoints, on the way between Da Nang and Hoi An.
Ruins of ancient Cham Hindu temples in the jungle; a UNESCO site.
Tall white Buddha statue at Linh Ung Pagoda on Son Tra, overlooking the bay.
Dragon-shaped bridge over the Han River that breathes fire and water.
Fire and water show on weekend nights
Da Nang's long, wide city beach.
UNESCO-listed old trading port: lantern-lit streets, street food, tailors, riverside cafés.
Ornate Chinese assembly hall and temple built by Fujian merchants.
Colorful Chinese temple honoring the general Guan Yu, across from the central market.
Hoi An's symbol: a small covered bridge from the early 1600s.
Dense maze of streets historically named for trades, packed with street food and shops, near Hoan Kiem Lake.
Narrow residential lane where trains pass inches from cafés.
Access is sometimes restricted by police
Ta Hien Street: a lively corner of tiny plastic stools and cheap fresh beer (bia hoi).
About 500 steps up to a dragon statue with sweeping views over the Tam Coc rice fields.
UNESCO-listed rowboat tours through limestone karsts and river caves.
Rowboat ride along a river through rice paddies and caves between limestone cliffs.
Upscale central district with cafés, cocktail bars, and the Yongkang Street food area.
Large leafy park, often called Taipei's Central Park.
World-class collection of Chinese imperial art and artifacts, incl. the famous Jadeite Cabbage.
Tea roaster in Dadaocheng since 1890; tastings, tea for sale, and tours of the roasting workshop.
Narrow hillside lanes of snack stalls, teahouses, and red lanterns.
Traditional teahouse in a historic building, with tea service and mountain views.
Short but steep hike near Jinguashi to a teapot-shaped rock with panoramic coastal views.
